analysis.one_liner: Taxes household wealth above $50 million at 2%, rising to 3% above $1 billion.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced in March 2024 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Ultra-Millionaire Tax Act of 2024 would create a new annual tax on the net value of everything a household owns — stocks, businesses, real estate, trusts, art — above $50 million, at 2 percent, rising to 3 percent on wealth above $1 billion. It would add anti-avoidance rules for assets parked in foreign trusts, steep penalties for undervaluing assets, mandatory audits of at least 30 percent of those subject to the tax each year, and $100 billion in new IRS enforcement funding over a decade. It never left the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit if the tax reduces the deficit or funds public spending without raising their own taxes. The roughly 100,000 households affected would pay; the bill would also fund IRS enforcement aimed at wealthy tax avoidance. The bill contains a built-in escalator: the top rate doubles to 6 percent if Congress ever enacts universal health coverage that bans duplicate private insurance.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone except households worth over $50 million

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an annual 2 percent tax on the net value of all assets of households above $50 million, and 3 percent above $1 billion, with no income-tax deduction for the wealth tax paid [S2].

Doubles the top rate to 6 percent in any year Congress enacts a universal health insurance program that bars private duplicate coverage — an explicit incentive tying the tax to Medicare-for-all-style legislation [S2].

Requires the IRS to audit at least 30 percent of taxpayers subject to the wealth tax every year, and authorizes $70 billion for enforcement, $10 billion for taxpayer services, and $20 billion for systems modernization for fiscal 2024-2034 [S2].

Cracks down on avoidance: assets moved to foreign corporations, partnerships, or trusts face new disclosure rules, gifts to young family members stay countable, and expatriates who renounce citizenship pay a 40 percent exit rate on their wealth [S2].
Undervaluing assets by 35 percent or more triggers penalties of 30 to 50 percent, and taxpayers facing genuine liquidity problems can get up to a five-year extension to pay [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The roughly 100,000 households with net worth above $50 million — mostly billionaires and centimillionaires — who would pay the new annual tax on their total assets, not just their income.

drawbacks.text: A wealth tax on unrealized gains is legally and practically untested in the United States; valuing private businesses, art, and other assets that do not trade publicly is hard, and the bill leaves the details to Treasury regulations to be written within 12 months of enactment [S2].

Because the tax applies to total net value rather than realized income, owners of illiquid businesses could owe tax on paper wealth before selling anything, though the bill allows payment deferrals of up to five years for severe liquidity constraints or hardship to an ongoing enterprise [S2].

Critics argue wealthy households and businesses would respond by relocating or restructuring assets — a risk the bill partly addresses with the 40 percent expatriation charge and foreign-trust rules, but which it cannot eliminate [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit to ordinary people is indirect: the tax itself falls only on the very richest households, and its value depends on how the revenue is used and how well the IRS can enforce it. The design takes valuation and avoidance seriously — mandatory audits, steep penalties for lowballing assets, exit taxes, and trust anti-avoidance rules — but the administrative burden is real and largely unresolved, resting on regulations not yet written. The core difficulty is political feasibility, which the bill's fate makes plain.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced S. 4017 on March 21, 2024, joined by seven senators — six Democrats and one Independent [S1].
The bill's only action was being read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S4].
No hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote ever took place, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households worth more than $50 million — none of them will pay the tax — and the tax-writing committee members who left it untouched.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wealthy households above the $50 million threshold

sides.party_line_note: All eight sponsors were Democrats plus one Independent; no Republican cosponsor appears on the bill, and it never advanced far enough for any vote.

industries.industry: Households with net worth above $50 million
industries.note: The bill would levy a new 2-3 percent annual tax on their total assets each year, with a 40 percent exit tax if they renounce citizenship. Fewer than 100,000 households are affected.

industries.industry: Private wealth management, trust, and estate-planning industry
industries.note: The bill's anti-avoidance rules — foreign trust disclosure, gifts-to-minors rules, mandatory audits — would reduce demand for structures built to shield large fortunes from tax. Advisers to the ultra-wealthy would lose business if it worked as designed.

The bill authorizes $100 billion over a decade for enforcement, taxpayer services, and modernization, plus a mandate to audit at least 30 percent of wealth-tax payers yearly. Stronger enforcement capacity serves taxpayers who pay what they owe.
